title: Formal courses or online self-study for learning skills
prompt:
Some people believe that the best way to learn a practical skill, such as cooking, coding or playing a musical instrument, is to take a formal course with a qualified teacher. Others think that free online videos and self-study are just as effective.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Give each view its own body paragraph and develop it with a reason and an example.
State your opinion in the introduction and keep it consistent to the conclusion.
A balanced or 'it depends' opinion is fine, but say clearly what it depends on.
Avoid 'In my opinion, I think'. Choose one.
Use specific examples (a guitar learner's wrist position, a cook's knife grip) rather than general statements.

samples.text:
Nowadays, many people want to learn new skills like cooking or programming. Some people think it is better to join a course with a teacher, but other people believe that online videos and studying alone is just as good. In this essay I will discuss both side and give my opinion.

On the one hand, a formal course have many advantages. The most important is that the teacher can correct the student mistakes immediately. For example, if someone is learning guitar and they hold it in the wrong way, a teacher can see it and help them. Also, in a course there is a fixed timetable, so students must come every week and they don't give up easily. However, courses are often expensive and not everyone can pay for them.

On the other hand, online videos are free and people can watch them anytime they want. There are millions of videos on the internet about every skill, so learners can choose the one they like. My cousin learned to make websites only from YouTube and now he is working as a web designer. Furthermore, people can repeat the video many times if they don't understand something, which is not possible in a class.

In my opinion, I think both ways are good but online learning is more better for most people because it is cheap and flexible. If people are serious they can learn by themselves. But for some skills like driving, it is necessary to have a teacher.

In conclusion, formal course and online videos both have advantages and disadvantages. I believe online learning is more suitable for most people nowadays, but sometimes a teacher is still needed.
samples.commentary: Task Response 6: both views are discussed and an opinion is given, but it shifts (online learning is 'more better', yet driving needs a teacher, which is not developed), and some support is generalised ('millions of videos about every skill'). Coherence & Cohesion 6: clear paragraphing, but linking is formulaic (On the one hand, Also, Furthermore) and 'In my opinion, I think' is redundant. Lexical Resource 6: adequate for the task, with repetition ('people', 'online videos') and an error ('more better'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy 6: a mix of simple and complex sentences, but frequent agreement and form errors ('a formal course have', 'videos and studying alone is', 'both side', 'the student mistakes', 'formal course'). Meaning is always clear.

samples.text:
Learning a practical skill once almost always meant enrolling in a class, but the internet now offers free tutorials on virtually any subject. While some argue that a qualified teacher remains essential, others claim that self-directed learning online can be equally effective. In my view, online resources are excellent for getting started, but a teacher becomes increasingly valuable as a learner progresses.

Those who favour formal courses point to the value of personalised feedback. A video cannot see what the learner is doing, so it cannot notice that a beginner pianist is developing a tense wrist or that a novice cook is consistently over-seasoning food. A good teacher spots these habits early, before they become difficult to correct. Courses also provide structure and accountability: having paid for a class and knowing that a teacher expects to see progress, students are more likely to practise regularly rather than abandon the skill after a few weeks.

On the other hand, supporters of self-study emphasise accessibility. Online videos cost nothing, can be watched at any time and can be paused or replayed as often as necessary, which suits for people with irregular working hours or limited budgets. The range of material is also enormous; a learner can compare several explanations of the same technique and choose the one that makes most sense to them. Many successful programmers, for instance, are entirely self-taught.

Personally, I believe the two approaches work best in combination. Videos are an efficient and low-risk way to discover whether a skill is worth pursuing and to master the basics. However, once a learner reaches the stage where small errors matter, the feedback of an expert is difficult to replace.

In conclusion, although online learning has made practical skills far more accessible, it complements formal teaching rather than replacing it.
samples.commentary: Task Response 7: both views are discussed and a clear position (start online, then seek a teacher) runs through the essay. Main ideas are extended well, although the self-taught programmers example is asserted rather than developed, and the conclusion is brief. Coherence & Cohesion 7: logical progression and a range of cohesive devices; each paragraph has a clear central idea. Lexical Resource 7: good topic vocabulary ('personalised feedback', 'accountability', 'self-directed'), used with some precision. Grammatical Range & Accuracy 7: a variety of complex structures, including participle clauses ('having paid for a class...'), with a few errors ('suits for people'). More fully supported examples and greater precision would move it towards 8.

samples.text:
The internet has made it possible to learn almost anything, from baking bread to writing software, without leaving home or paying a fee. This has prompted a debate about whether formal tuition with a qualified teacher still offers anything that free videos and independent study cannot. I would argue that while self-study is remarkably effective for acquiring knowledge, it is weaker at developing the judgement that distinguishes a competent practitioner from a skilled one.

The case for self-teaching is strong. Online tutorials remove the two greatest barriers to learning, cost and time, so that a shift worker can learn to code at midnight and a student on a tight budget can learn the guitar without paying for lessons. Learners can also move at their own pace, skipping what they already understand and replaying difficult sections as often as they need to. Moreover, the sheer volume of material means that if one explanation fails, another is a click away. For many people, these advantages make the difference between learning a skill and never attempting it at all.

Advocates of formal courses, however, highlight something that videos cannot provide: feedback on the learner's own performance. A tutorial can demonstrate how to hold a knife, but it cannot see that the viewer is holding theirs dangerously. In skills where physical technique matters, uncorrected faults quickly become ingrained habits, and these can take far longer to unlearn than they took to acquire. A teacher also sequences material deliberately, ensuring that foundations are secure before new demands are introduced, whereas self-taught learners often have gaps they are unaware of.

On balance, I believe the most effective route is to begin independently and to seek expert guidance once progress starts to stall. In that sense, the two approaches are not rivals but successive stages of the same journey, and online learning has made formal teaching more targeted rather than obsolete.
samples.commentary: Task Response 8: a nuanced position (self-study builds knowledge; teachers build judgement) is stated early and developed with relevant, specific examples such as the knife grip and ingrained habits. Coherence & Cohesion 8: paragraphs are sequenced logically, and cohesion is managed naturally without overused connectors. Lexical Resource 8: wide and precise ('ingrained habits', 'sequences material deliberately', 'obsolete'), with an occasional informal phrase ('a click away'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy 8: a wide range of structures with no noticeable errors. It is not a 9 because the introduction is rather long and the opposing view could be weighed more explicitly in the conclusion.
